parts.problem_md:
Calcium phosphate is a sparingly soluble naturally occurring mineral that is a large component of bones and teeth. The *K*<sub>sp</sub> value at 25 °C for calcium phosphate is 2.07 x 10<sup>-33</sup>.

Construct an equation to show the equilibrium present in a saturated solution of calcium phosphate. Include state symbols.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equilibrium equation for the dissolution of calcium phosphate is:
> 
> - Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (s) ⇌ 3Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required; equation must be balanced with 3:2 stoichiometry (Ca<sup>2+</sup> to PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup>)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Calcium phosphate contains Ca<sup>2+</sup> (charge 2+) and PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (charge 3-). Three Ca<sup>2+</sup> ions and two PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> ions balance the charges (6+ = 6-), giving the formula Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Calcium phosphate is a sparingly soluble naturally occurring mineral that is a large component of bones and teeth. The Ksp value at 25 °C for calcium phosphate is 2.07 x 10^-33.

The equilibrium equation for the dissolution of calcium phosphate is:
Ca3(PO4)2 (s) ⇌ 3Ca^2+ (aq) + 2PO4^3- (aq)

Use your answer to part **(a)** to calculate the concentration, in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, of the calcium and phosphate ions in solution. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the concentrations of ions in a saturated solution of calcium phosphate:

- Let *x* = solubility of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, so [Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = 3*x* and [PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq)] = 2*x*

- Write the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression and substitute:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)]<sup>3</sup>[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup>

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = (3*x*)<sup>3</sup>(2*x*)<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Expand and set equal to *K*<sub>sp</sub>:

2.07 x 10<sup>-33</sup> = 27*x*<sup>3</sup> x 4*x*<sup>2</sup>

2.07 x 10<sup>-33</sup> = 108*x*<sup>5</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Solve for *x*:

*x*<sup>5</sup> = $\frac{2.07\times10^{-33}}{108}$

*x*<sup>5</sup> = 1.92 x 10<sup>-35</sup>

*x* = `\sqrt[5]{1.92 \times 10^{-35}}`

*x* = 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the equilibrium concentrations:

[Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = 3 x 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> = **3.42 x 10**<sup>**-7**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>

[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq)] = 2 x 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> = **2.28 x 10**<sup>**-7**</sup>** mol dm**<sup>**-3**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = (3*x*)<sup>3</sup>(2*x*)<sup>2</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for 108*x*<sup>5</sup> = 2.07 x 10<sup>-33</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *x* = 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for both concentrations: [Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = 3.42 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND **[PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> (aq)] = 2.28 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> Express each ion concentration in terms of *x* (the solubility).
> 
> Since Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> gives 3 Ca<sup>2+</sup> and 2 PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup> per formula unit, [Ca<sup>2+</sup>] = 3*x*<sup>3</sup> and [PO<sub>4</sub><sup>3-</sup>] = 2*x*<sup>*2*</sup>*. *

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Let x = solubility of Ca~3~(PO~4~)~2~, so [Ca^2+^ (aq)] = 3x and [PO~4~^3-^ (aq)] = 2x

x = 1.14 x 10^-7^ mol dm^-3^

[Ca^2+^ (aq)] = 3 x 1.14 x 10^-7^ = 3.42 x 10^-7^ mol dm^-3^

[PO~4~^3-^ (aq)] = 2 x 1.14 x 10^-7^ = 2.28 x 10^-7^ mol dm^-3^

Use your answer to part **(b)** to calculate the mass of solute, in grams, in 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of solution at 25 °C. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the mass of calcium phosphate, Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, dissolved in 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of solution:

- Use *x* = 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (solubility of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) to find moles in 150 cm<sup>3</sup>:

*n*(Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = 1.14 x 10<sup>-7</sup> x 0.150

*n*(Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = 1.71 x 10<sup>-8</sup> mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the mass (*M*<sub>r</sub> of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> = 310.3):

mass = 1.71 x 10<sup>-8</sup> x 310.3

mass = **5.31 x 10**<sup>**-6**</sup> g **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *n*(Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>) = 1.71 x 10<sup>-8</sup> mol
> 
> 1 mark for mass = 5.31 x 10<sup>-6</sup> g
> 
> Allow 5.30 x 10<sup>-6</sup> g depending on *M*<sub>r</sub> used
> 
> Allow error carried forward from part (b) if *x* is used consistently

> **[exam-tip]**
> The value of *x* from part (b) is the molar solubility of Ca<sub>3</sub>(PO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub> in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.
> 
> Convert 150 cm<sup>3</sup> to 0.150 dm<sup>3</sup>, multiply by *x* to get moles, then multiply by *M*<sub>r</sub> to get mass.

parts.problem_md:
The *K*<sub>sp</sub> value for silver bromide, AgBr (s) is 3.3 x 10<sup>-13</sup> at 298 K.

Construct an equation to show the equilibrium present in a saturated solution of silver bromide. Include state symbols.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equilibrium equation for a saturated solution of silver bromide is:
> 
> - AgBr (s) ⇌ Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Br<sup>–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Silver bromide dissolves to give one Ag<sup>+</sup> ion and one Br<sup>–</sup> ion per formula unit. Including state symbols, (s) for the undissolved solid and (aq) for the dissolved ions, is required for the mark.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The *K*~sp~ value for silver bromide, AgBr (s) is 3.3 x 10^-13^ at 298 K.

Construct an equation to show the equilibrium present in a saturated solution of silver bromide. Include state symbols.

The equilibrium equation for a saturated solution of silver bromide is:

AgBr (s) ⇌ Ag^+^ (aq) + Br^–^ (aq)

State and explain the effect on the concentration of dissolved silver ions when sodium bromide solution is added to a saturated solution of silver bromide.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The effect on the concentration of dissolved silver ions when sodium bromide solution is added:
> 
> - Decreases **[1 mark]**
> - The increase in [Br<sup>–</sup> (aq)] shifts the equilibrium to the left (towards AgBr (s)) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is an application of Le Chatelier’s principle. Adding sodium bromide increases the Br<sup>–</sup> concentration. To oppose this change, the equilibrium shifts left, consuming both Ag<sup>+</sup> and Br<sup>–</sup> ions and forming more AgBr (s), so [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] decreases.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The *K*~sp~ value for silver bromide, AgBr (s) is 3.3 x 10^-13^ at 298 K.

Calculate the concentration, in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, of silver ions at 298 K in a saturated solution of silver bromide. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the concentration of silver ions in a saturated solution of silver bromide:

- Let *s* = solubility of AgBr = [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = [Br<sup>–</sup> (aq)]

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)][Br<sup>–</sup> (aq)] = *s*<sup>2</sup> = 3.3 x 10<sup>-13</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Solve for *s*:

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = $\sqrt{3.3\times10^{-13}}$

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = **5.74 x 10**<sup>**-7**</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup> = 3.3 x 10<sup>-13</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = 5.74 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> Allow 5.7 x 10<sup>-7</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (2 sf)

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a 1:1 salt such as AgBr, the two ion concentrations in a saturated solution are equal (both equal to the solubility *s*), so *K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup>. Taking the square root gives the concentration of each ion.

parts.problem_md:
The feasibility of a chemical reaction depends on the standard Gibbs free energy change, Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup>. This is dependent on the standard enthalpy and entropy changes, and the temperature.

State and explain whether the following processes will lead to an increase or decrease in entropy.

i) the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid

[1]

ii) the dissolving of solid potassium chloride in water

[1]

iii) the condensing of water from steam

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid:
> 
> - Entropy increases
> **AND**
> A gas (H<sub>2</sub>) is produced **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The dissolving of solid potassium chloride in water:
> 
> - Entropy increases
> **AND**
> The ordered solid lattice breaks down to give freely moving ions in solution **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The condensing of water from steam:
> 
> - Entropy decreases
> **AND**
> The number of moles of gas decreases / a more ordered liquid is formed **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Entropy is a measure of disorder. Processes that produce gases, dissolve solids, or increase the number of particles increase entropy. Processes that convert gases to liquids or reduce the number of particles decrease entropy.

parts.problem_md:
Magnesium carbonate can be decomposed on heating.

MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) → MgO (s) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)      Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> = +117 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>

Standard entropies are shown in Table 2.1.

**Table 2.1**

| **substance** | MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) | MgO (s) | CO<sub>2</sub> (g) |
|---|---|---|---|
| *S*<sup>ɵ</sup> / J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> | +65.7 | +26.9 | +214 |

i) Calculate Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> for this reaction at 298 K. Show your working.

[3]

ii) Explain why this reaction is feasible only at high temperatures.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> for the decomposition of MgCO<sub>3</sub> at 298 K:

- Calculate Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup>:

Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> = Σ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup>(products) – Σ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup>(reactants)

Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> = (26.9 + 214) – 65.7

Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> = **+175.2** J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute into the Gibbs equation:

Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> **[1 mark]**

Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = 117 – (298 x $\frac{175.2}{1000}$)

Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = **+64.8** kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) 1 mark for Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> = +175.2 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for correct application of Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = +64.8 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup> (to at least 3 sf)

> **[exam-tip]**
> Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> is in J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup> while Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> is in kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>. Divide Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> by 1000 before substituting to ensure consistent units.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) This reaction is feasible only at high temperatures because:
> 
> - *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> exceeds Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup>
> **AND**
> Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> becomes negative **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> (+117 kJ mol<sup>–1</sup>) and Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> (+175.2 J K<sup>–1</sup> mol<sup>–1</sup>) are positive. Δ*G*<sup>ɵ</sup> = Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup> – *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> only becomes negative (feasible) when *T* is large enough that *T*Δ*S*<sup>ɵ</sup> > Δ*H*<sup>ɵ</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
Table 2.2 lists values of solubility products, *K*<sub>**sp**</sub>, of some Group 2 carbonates.

**Table 2.2**

| carbonate | **solubility product in water at 298 K, *****K***<sub>**sp **</sub>**/ mol**<sup>**2**</sup>** dm**<sup>**–6**</sup> |
|---|---|
| MgCO<sub>3</sub> | 1.0 × 10<sup>–5</sup> |
| CaCO<sub>3</sub> | 5.0 × 10<sup>–9</sup> |
| SrCO<sub>3</sub> | 1.1 × 10<sup>–10</sup> |

Deduce the trend in the solubility of the Group 2 carbonates down the group. Justify your answer using the data given.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The trend in solubility of the Group 2 carbonates down the group:
> 
> - Solubility decreases down the group
> **AND**
> *K*<sub>sp</sub> decreases down the group (justified by reference to data in Table 2.2) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> *K*<sub>sp</sub> values with more negative exponents represent smaller numbers and indicate lower solubility. MgCO<sub>3</sub> (*K*<sub>sp</sub> = 1.0 × 10<sup>–5</sup>) is the most soluble; SrCO<sub>3</sub> (*K*<sub>sp</sub> = 1.1 × 10<sup>–10</sup>) is the least soluble.

parts.problem_md:
i) Construct an equation to show the equilibrium for the solubility product of MgCO<sub>3</sub>. Include state symbols.

[1]

ii) With reference to your equation in **(d)(i)**, state what is observed when a few cm<sup>3</sup> of concentrated Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) are added to a saturated solution of MgCO<sub>3</sub>. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equilibrium equation for the solubility product of MgCO<sub>3</sub> is:
> 
> - MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) ⇌ Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols are required; do not accept + (aq) in the equation

> **[exam-tip]**
> MgCO<sub>3</sub> dissolves to give one Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion and one CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> ion. The solid MgCO<sub>3</sub> is on the left of the equilibrium; the aqueous ions are on the right. A "+ (aq)" term is not required and is not accepted.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) When concentrated Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (aq) is added to a saturated MgCO<sub>3</sub> solution:
> 
> - A white solid / precipitate (of MgCO<sub>3</sub>) forms **[1 mark]**
> - Adding Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> increases [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq)], which shifts the equilibrium to the left **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> provides additional CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> ions. By Le Chatelier’s principle, the equilibrium shifts left to reduce [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup>], consuming Mg<sup>2+</sup> and CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> ions and depositing more solid MgCO<sub>3</sub> as a precipitate.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Table 2.2 lists values of solubility products, *K*~**sp**~, of some Group 2 carbonates.

**Table 2.2**

| carbonate | **solubility product in water at 298 K, *****K***~**sp **~**/ mol**^**2**^** dm**^**–6**^ |
| --- | :---: |
| MgCO~3~ | 1.0 × 10^–5^ |
| CaCO~3~ | 5.0 × 10^–9^ |
| SrCO~3~ | 1.1 × 10^–10^ |

Use the data in Table 2.2 to calculate the solubility of MgCO<sub>3</sub> in water at 298 K, in g dm<sup>–3</sup>. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the solubility of MgCO<sub>3</sub> in water at 298 K:

- Let *s* = solubility = [Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = [CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> (aq)]

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup> = 1.0 x 10<sup>–5</sup>

*s* = $\sqrt{1.0\times10^{-5}}$ = 3.2 x 10<sup>–3</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Convert to g dm<sup>–3</sup> (*M*<sub>r</sub> of MgCO<sub>3</sub> = 84.3):

solubility = 3.2 x 10<sup>–3</sup> x 84.3

solubility = **0.27 g dm**<sup>**–3**</sup>** ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *s* = 3.2 x 10<sup>–3</sup> mol dm<sup>–3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for solubility = 0.27 g dm<sup>–3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a 1:1 salt like MgCO<sub>3</sub>, *K*<sub>sp</sub> = *s*<sup>2</sup>. Take the square root of *K*<sub>sp</sub> to find the molar solubility, then multiply by *M*<sub>r</sub> to convert to g dm<sup>–3</sup>.

parts.problem_md: Describe and explain the variation in the thermal stabilities of the carbonates of the Group 2 elements.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The variation in thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates:
> 
> - Thermal stability increases down the group
> - The ionic radius of the M<sup>2+</sup> cation increases down the group
> - There is less distortion / polarisation of the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> anion
> - Less weakening of the C–O bonds in the carbonate ion
> 
> **[3 marks]**
> 
> Any three chemical ideas score 2 marks
> 
> Any two chemical ideas score 1 mark

> **[exam-tip]**
> As ionic radius increases down Group 2, charge density of the M<sup>2+</sup> cation decreases. A smaller cation has greater polarising ability and distorts the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2–</sup> anion more strongly, weakening C–O bonds and lowering the decomposition temperature.

parts.problem_md:
A saturated solution of silver(I) chloride has a solubility of 1.46 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

Write the expression for the solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, for silver(I) chloride.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The expression for the solubility product of silver(I) chloride is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)][Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)] **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols (aq) are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> When writing a *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression, consider the dissolution equation:
> 
> AgCl (s) ⇌ Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)
> 
> The *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression is the product of the ionic concentrations in square brackets.
> 
> For compounds that produce ions with different stoichiometric coefficients, raise each term to the power of its coefficient. For example, for MgCl<sub>2</sub>:
> 
> *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq)][Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup>

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

A saturated solution of silver(I) chloride has a solubility of 1.46 x 10^-3^ mol dm^-3^.

Write the expression for the solubility product, *K*~sp~, for silver(I) chloride.

Using the information and your answer to part **(a)**, calculate the value of *K*<sub>sp</sub> for silver(I) chloride. State the units of *K*<sub>sp</sub>. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, of silver(I) chloride:

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = [1.46 x 10<sup>-3</sup>][1.46 x 10<sup>-3</sup>]

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = **2.13 x 10**<sup>**-6**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- State the units:

units = mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = 2.13 x 10<sup>-6</sup>
> 
> Allow 2.1 x 10<sup>-6</sup> (2 sf)
> 
> 1 mark for units = mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> To determine the units of *K*<sub>sp</sub>, substitute mol dm<sup>-3</sup> for each concentration term and multiply the powers:
> 
> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> x mol dm<sup>-3</sup> = mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

parts.problem_md:
A saturated solution of iron(II) hydroxide has a solubility of 5.82 x 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>.

i) Write the expression for the solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, for iron(II) hydroxide.

[1]

ii) Calculate the solubility product and units for iron(II) hydroxide. Show your working.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The expression for the solubility product of iron(II) hydroxide is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq)][OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols (aq) are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> For Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>, the dissolution equation is Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) ⇌ Fe<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>–</sup> (aq). The [OH<sup>–</sup>] term is raised to the power of 2 in the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression.

ii) To calculate the solubility product and units for iron(II) hydroxide:

- Note that [OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)] = 2 x solubility of Fe(OH)<sub>2</sub>:

[OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)] = 2 x 5.82 x 10<sup>-6</sup>

[OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)] = 1.164 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = [5.82 x 10<sup>-6</sup>][2 x 5.82 x 10<sup>-6</sup>]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = **7.89 x 10**<sup>**-16**</sup> **[1 mark]**

- State the units:

units = mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow *K*<sub>sp</sub> = 7.88 x 10<sup>-16</sup> or 7.9 x 10<sup>-16</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> To determine the units of *K*<sub>sp</sub> with three concentration terms, substitute mol dm<sup>-3</sup> for each:
> 
> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> x (mol dm<sup>-3</sup>)<sup>2</sup> = mol<sup>3</sup> dm<sup>-9</sup>

parts.problem_md:
The general equilibrium expression for the partition coefficient is:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = `\frac{\left[\text{equilibrium concentration in organic layer / mol dm}^{-3}\right]}{\left[\text{equilibrium concentration in aqueous layer / mol dm}^{-3}\right]}`

100 cm<sup>3</sup> of a 0.500 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> aqueous solution of ethylamine, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, was shaken with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of an organic solvent at 25 °C and allowed to reach equilibrium.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq) ⇌ CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic solvent)

Only 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of the aqueous layer was removed and titrated against 0.500 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> hydrochloric acid. 15.0 cm<sup>3</sup> was required to reach the end point.

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq) + HCl (aq) → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> (aq) + Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq)

Calculate the partition coefficient, *K*<sub>pc</sub>, of ethylamine between the organic solvent and water. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the partition coefficient, *K*<sub>pc</sub>, of ethylamine between the organic solvent and water:

- Calculate the moles of ethylamine in the 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> aliquot from the titration:

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) = *n*(HCl)

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) = 0.500 x 0.0150

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) = 7.50 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol

- The aliquot was 50.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 100 cm<sup>3</sup> total aqueous layer, so total moles in the aqueous layer:

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (aq) = 2 x 7.50 x 10<sup>-3</sup>

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (aq) = 0.0150 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the total initial moles of ethylamine and hence the moles in the organic layer:

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (total) = 0.500 x 0.100

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (total) = 0.0500 mol

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (organic) = 0.0500 - 0.0150

*n*(CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) (organic) = 0.0350 mol

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the equilibrium concentrations in each layer (volume of each layer = 100 cm<sup>3</sup> = 0.100 dm<sup>3</sup>):

[CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq)] = $\frac{0.0150}{0.100}$

[CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq)] = 0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic)] = $\frac{0.0350}{0.100}$

[CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic)] = 0.350 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the partition coefficient:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = $\frac{0.350}{0.150}$

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = **2.33**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for total moles of ethylamine in aqueous layer = 0.0150 mol
> 
> 1 mark for moles of ethylamine in organic layer = 0.0350 mol
> 
> 1 mark for both concentrations correct: [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (aq)] = 0.150 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> AND [CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub> (organic)] = 0.350 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 2.33
> 
> Allow 2.3 (2 sf)

> **[exam-tip]**
> A common error is to treat the aliquot volume (50.0 cm<sup>3</sup>) as the total aqueous layer. The moles from the titration must be doubled because only half the aqueous layer was titrated.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The general equilibrium expression for the partition coefficient is:

Kpc = [equilibrium concentration in organic layer / mol dm^-3] / [equilibrium concentration in aqueous layer / mol dm^-3]

Kpc = 2.33

Use your answer to part **(a)** to state whether ethylamine is more soluble in the aqueous or organic solvent. Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Whether ethylamine is more soluble in the aqueous or organic solvent:
> 
> - Organic solvent **[1 mark]**
> - The value of *K*<sub>pc</sub> is greater than 1 **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When *K*<sub>pc</sub> > 1, the equilibrium concentration is greater in the organic layer, so the solute (ethylamine) is more soluble in the organic solvent.
> 
> When *K*<sub>pc</sub> < 1, the solute is more soluble in water.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The general equilibrium expression for the partition coefficient is:

*K*~pc~ = [equilibrium concentration in organic layer / mol dm⁻³] / [equilibrium concentration in aqueous layer / mol dm⁻³]

A solution containing 1.00 g of compound **A** in 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of water was shaken with 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of ether and allowed to reach equilibrium. 0.60 g of compound **A** is present in the ether layer at equilibrium.

Calculate the partition coefficient of compound **A** between ether and water. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the partition coefficient of compound **A** between ether and water:

- Write the *K*<sub>pc</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = [compound **A** (ether)] / [compound **A** (aq)]

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the concentration in each layer:

[compound **A** (ether)] = $\frac{0.60}{0.010}$ = 60 g dm<sup>-3</sup>

[compound **A** (aq)] = $\frac{0.40}{0.100}$ = 4.0 g dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the partition coefficient:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = $\frac{60}{4.0}$

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = **15**

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>pc</sub> expression with ether as numerator and aqueous as denominator
> 
> 1 mark for both concentrations: [compound **A** (ether)] = 60 g dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND **[compound **A** (aq)] = 4.0 g dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 15

> **[exam-tip]**
> Note that 0.60 g of compound **A** is present in 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of ether (not 100 cm<sup>3</sup>). The mass remaining in the aqueous layer is 1.00 - 0.60 = 0.40 g. Convert volumes to dm<sup>3</sup> before calculating concentrations.

parts.problem_md:
This question is about solubility products.

A 1.70 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> solution of calcium nitrate is mixed with an equal volume of 1.50 x 10<sup>-3</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> potassium sulfate.

Calculate the ionic product and state whether calcium sulfate (*K*<sub>sp</sub> = 2.00 x 10<sup>-5</sup>) will precipitate. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the ionic product and determine whether calcium sulfate will precipitate:

- When equal volumes are mixed, each concentration is halved:

[Ca<sup>2+</sup> (aq)] = $\frac{1.70\times10^{-3}}{2}$ = 8.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)] = $\frac{1.50\times10^{-3}}{2}$ = 7.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the ionic product:

IP = [Ca<sup>2+</sup>][SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = 8.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> x 7.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup>

IP = **6.38 x 10**<sup>**-7**</sup> mol<sup>2</sup> dm<sup>-6</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Compare IP with *K*<sub>sp</sub>:

6.38 x 10<sup>-7</sup> < 2.00 x 10<sup>-5</sup>

There will be no precipitation as IP < *K*<sub>sp</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both concentrations after mixing: [Ca<sup>2+</sup>] = 8.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND **[SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = 7.50 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for IP = 6.38 x 10<sup>-7</sup> (allow 6.375 x 10<sup>-7</sup>)
> 
> 1 mark for IP < *K*<sub>sp</sub> **AND **a conclusion of no precipitation

> **[exam-tip]**
> When equal volumes of two solutions are mixed, the total volume doubles so each concentration is halved.
> 
> Calculate the ionic product (IP) using these diluted concentrations, then compare with *K*<sub>sp</sub>: if IP > *K*<sub>sp</sub>, a precipitate forms; if IP < *K*<sub>sp</sub>, no precipitate forms.

parts.problem_md:
Water with a manganese ion, Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq), concentration above 1.8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> will cause clothes to stain when being washed. The manganese can precipitate as Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) which has a *K*<sub>sp</sub> of 4.5 x 10<sup>-14</sup>. This reduces the concentration of Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) by the addition of OH<sup>–</sup> ions.

i) Write the expression for *K*<sub>sp</sub>.

[1]

ii) Calculate the concentration of OH<sup>–</sup> ions. Show your working.

[2]

iii) Calculate the minimum pH at 298 K required to prevent clothes from being stained.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression for Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Mn<sup>2+</sup> (aq)][OH<sup>–</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Mn(OH)<sub>2</sub> dissociates to give one Mn<sup>2+</sup> ion and two OH<sup>–</sup> ions. The [OH<sup>–</sup>] term must be raised to the power of 2.

ii) To calculate the concentration of OH<sup>–</sup> ions:

- Substitute [Mn<sup>2+</sup>] = 1.8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

4.5 x 10<sup>-14</sup> = 1.8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> x [OH<sup>–</sup>]<sup>2</sup> **[1 mark]**

[OH<sup>–</sup>]<sup>2</sup> = $\frac{4.5\times10^{-14}}{1.8\times10^{-6}}$ = 2.5 x 10<sup>-8</sup>

[OH<sup>–</sup>] = **1.58 x 10**<sup>**-4**</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = 1.8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> x [OH<sup>–</sup>]<sup>2</sup> or equivalent rearrangement
> 
> 1 mark for [OH<sup>–</sup>] = 1.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

iii) To calculate the minimum pH at 298 K:

- Calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] using *K*<sub>w</sub>:

[H<sup>+</sup>] = `\frac{K_w}{[\text{OH}^-]}` = $\frac{1.00\times10^{-14}}{1.58\times10^{-4}}$ = 6.33 x 10<sup>-11</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

pH = –log(6.33 x 10<sup>-11</sup>)

pH = **10.2** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii)
> 
> 1 mark for [H<sup>+</sup>] = `\frac{K_w}{[\text{OH}^-]}` **OR **[H<sup>+</sup>] = $\frac{1.00\times10^{-14}}{1.58\times10^{-4}}$
> 
> 1 mark for pH = 10.2
> 
> Allow pH calculated as 14 + log(1.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup>) = 10.2

> **[exam-tip]**
> For the pH calculation, *K*<sub>w</sub> = [H<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>–</sup>] is found in the data booklet at 298 K. Calculate [H<sup>+</sup>] = *K*<sub>w</sub> / [OH<sup>–</sup>], then apply pH = –log[H<sup>+</sup>].
> 
> Alternatively, pOH = –log[OH<sup>–</sup>] = 3.80, and pH = 14 – pOH = 10.2.

parts.problem_md:
Consider the following equilibrium in a saturated solution of AgBr (s):

AgBr (s) ⇌ Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq) + Br<sup>–</sup> (aq)

Explain what will happen to the solubility of AgBr (s) when each of the following substances is added to the solution.

i) AgNO<sub>3</sub>

[2]

ii) Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) When AgNO<sub>3</sub> is added to the saturated solution:
> 
> - Added Ag<sup>+</sup> ions increase [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] (common ion effect) **[1 mark]**
> - Equilibrium shifts to the left towards AgBr (s), reducing the solubility of AgBr **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) When Pb(NO<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> is added to the saturated solution:
> 
> - Pb<sup>2+</sup> ions react with Br<sup>–</sup> ions to form insoluble PbBr<sub>2</sub>, removing Br<sup>–</sup> from the equilibrium **[1 mark]**
> - Equilibrium shifts to the right, increasing the solubility of AgBr **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a common ion (Ag<sup>+</sup> or Br<sup>–</sup>) is added, the ionic product exceeds *K*<sub>sp</sub> and the equilibrium shifts left, reducing solubility. When Pb<sup>2+</sup> is added, it forms insoluble PbBr<sub>2</sub>, removing Br<sup>–</sup> and shifting the equilibrium right, increasing solubility.

parts.problem_md: Explain why more Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> dissolves when hydrochloric acid is added to a saturated solution of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why more Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> dissolves when hydrochloric acid is added to a saturated solution:
> 
> - H<sup>+</sup> ions from HCl react with OH<sup>–</sup> ions, removing them from solution (forming H<sub>2</sub>O) **[1 mark]**
> - Equilibrium shifts to the right, increasing the solubility of Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Adding H<sup>+</sup> ions from a strong acid removes OH<sup>–</sup> ions from solution via neutralisation. By Le Chatelier’s principle, the equilibrium Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub> (s) ⇌ Mg<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + 2OH<sup>–</sup> (aq) shifts right to restore [OH<sup>–</sup>], dissolving more Mg(OH)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
i) State what is meant by partition coefficient.

[2]

ii) Ammonia is soluble in both water and organic solvents.

An aqueous solution of ammonia is shaken with the immiscible organic solvent trichloromethane. The mixture is left to reach equilibrium.

Samples are taken from each layer and titrated with dilute hydrochloric acid.

- A 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> sample from the trichloromethane layer requires 13.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> HCl to reach the end-point.
- A 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> sample from the aqueous layer requires 12.5 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol dm<sup>–3</sup> HCl to reach the end-point.

Calculate the partition coefficient, *K*<sub>pc</sub>, of ammonia between trichloromethane and water. Show your working.

[3]

iii) Butylamine, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>, is also soluble in both water and organic solvents. Suggest how the numerical value of *K*<sub>pc</sub> of butylamine between trichloromethane and water would compare to the value of *K*<sub>pc</sub> calculated in **(a)(ii)**. Explain your answer.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The partition coefficient is:
> 
> - The ratio of the concentrations of a solute in two immiscible solvents **[1 mark]**
> - At equilibrium **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The partition coefficient expression is *K*<sub>pc</sub> = [solute in organic layer] / [solute in aqueous layer], evaluated once equilibrium is established.

ii) To calculate the partition coefficient, *K*<sub>pc</sub>, of ammonia between trichloromethane and water:

- Calculate [NH<sub>3</sub>] in the aqueous layer:

[NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)] = 0.100 x $\frac{12.5}{10.0}$ = 0.125 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate [NH<sub>3</sub>] in the trichloromethane layer:

[NH<sub>3</sub> (organic)] = 0.100 x $\frac{13.0}{25.0}$ = 0.052 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the partition coefficient:

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = $\frac{0.052}{0.125}$

*K*<sub>pc</sub> = **0.416** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) 1 mark for [NH<sub>3</sub> (aq)] = 0.125 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for [NH<sub>3</sub> (organic)] = 0.052 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 0.416
> 
> *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 0.125/0.052 = 2.40 is also accepted if the aqueous layer is used as numerator consistently

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find [NH<sub>3</sub>] in each layer: c = c(HCl) x V(HCl) / V(sample). The Ksp value of 0.416 < 1, meaning ammonia is more soluble in the aqueous layer than in trichloromethane.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> iii) How the *K*<sub>pc</sub> of butylamine between trichloromethane and water compares:
> 
> - If *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 0.416 (organic/aqueous): the *K*<sub>pc</sub> for butylamine is larger than for ammonia
> **OR**
> If *K*<sub>pc</sub> = 2.40 (aqueous/organic): the *K*<sub>pc</sub> for butylamine is smaller than for ammonia **[1 mark]**
> - Butylamine contains a hydrophobic / non-polar butyl (C<sub>4</sub>) chain
> **AND**
> Butylamine is therefore more soluble in trichloromethane than ammonia is **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Butylamine has a longer non-polar hydrocarbon chain compared to ammonia, making it more hydrophobic. Non-polar molecules dissolve preferentially in non-polar organic solvents such as trichloromethane, increasing the relative concentration in the organic layer.

parts.problem_md: Butanamide, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>CONH<sub>2</sub>, is much less basic than butylamine. Explain why.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Why butanamide is much less basic than butylamine:
> 
> - The lone pair on the nitrogen atom is delocalised into the adjacent C=O group / forms part of the extended π system **[1 mark]**
> - The lone pair is therefore less available to accept a proton **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In amines such as butylamine, the lone pair on nitrogen is localised and readily available to donate to a proton, making them moderately basic. In amides such as butanamide, partial delocalisation of the N lone pair into the adjacent C=O π system significantly reduces its availability, which is why amides are far less basic than amines.

parts.problem_md:
Silver chromate, Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>, is a chemical compound of silver and hexavalent chromium that is used in photography.

It has a solubility product, *K*<sub>sp</sub>, of 9.0 x 10<sup>-12</sup> at 25 °C.

Write the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression for Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression for Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> is:
> 
> - *K*<sub>sp</sub> = [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)]<sup>2</sup>[CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)] **[1 mark]**
> 
> [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] must be squared
> 
> State symbols (aq) are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> dissociates to give two Ag<sup>+</sup> ions and one CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> ion. The concentration of Ag<sup>+</sup> must be raised to the power of 2 in the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Silver chromate, Ag~2~CrO~4~, is a chemical compound of silver and hexavalent chromium that is used in photography.

It has a solubility product, *K*~sp~, of 9.0 x 10^-12^ at 25 °C.

Write the *K*~sp~ expression for Ag~2~CrO~4~.

The *K*~sp~ expression for Ag~2~CrO~4~ is:

*K*~sp~ = [Ag^+^ (aq)]^2^[CrO~4~^2-^ (aq)]

Use your answer to part **(a)** to calculate the solubility, in mol dm<sup>-3</sup>, of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> (aq). Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> in 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> (aq):

- Let *s* = solubility of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>; [Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = 2*s* and [CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)] ≈ 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> (common ion)

- Substitute into the *K*<sub>sp</sub> expression:

*K*<sub>sp</sub> = (2*s*)<sup>2</sup> x 0.020 = 9.0 x 10<sup>-12</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and solve:

4*s*<sup>2</sup> = $\frac{9.0\times10^{-12}}{0.020}$ = 4.5 x 10<sup>-10</sup> **[1 mark]**

*s*<sup>2</sup> = 1.125 x 10<sup>-10</sup>

*s* = $\sqrt{1.125\times10^{-10}}$ = **1.06 x 10**<sup>**-5**</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for *K*<sub>sp</sub> = (2*s*)<sup>2</sup> x 0.020 (correct substitution with common ion)
> 
> 1 mark for 4*s*<sup>2</sup> = 4.5 x 10<sup>-10</sup> or equivalent rearrangement
> 
> 1 mark for *s* = 1.06 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> In the presence of a common ion (CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> from K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub>), the [CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] is approximated as 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> since the Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> contribution is negligible.
> 
> Substituting [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = 2*s* and [CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = 0.020 gives *K*<sub>sp</sub> = 4*s*<sup>2</sup> x 0.020.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Silver chromate, Ag₂CrO₄, is a chemical compound of silver and hexavalent chromium that is used in photography.

It has a solubility product, *K*sp, of 9.0 x 10⁻¹² at 25 °C.

10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1.0 x 10<sup>-4</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> AgNO<sub>3</sub> (aq) was mixed with 10.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.020 mol dm<sup>-3</sup> K<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> (aq).

Calculate the ionic product of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> and state whether a precipitate of silver chromate will form. Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To determine whether a precipitate of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> will form on mixing:

- Calculate the concentrations after mixing (total volume = 10.0 + 10.0 = 20.0 cm<sup>3</sup>):

[Ag<sup>+</sup> (aq)] = $\frac{1.0\times10^{-4}\times10.0}{20.0}$ = 5.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

[CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup> (aq)] = $\frac{0.020\times10.0}{20.0}$ = 0.010 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Calculate the ionic product:

IP = [Ag<sup>+</sup>]<sup>2</sup>[CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = (5.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup>)<sup>2</sup> x 0.010

IP = **2.5 x 10**<sup>**-11**</sup>

**[1 mark]**

- Compare IP with *K*<sub>sp</sub>:

2.5 x 10<sup>-11</sup> > 9.0 x 10<sup>-12</sup>

A precipitate of Ag<sub>2</sub>CrO<sub>4</sub> will form because IP > *K*<sub>sp</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for both concentrations after mixing: [Ag<sup>+</sup>] = 5.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> mol dm<sup>-3</sup> **AND **[CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>] = 0.010 mol dm<sup>-3</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for IP = 2.5 x 10<sup>-11</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for IP > *K*<sub>sp</sub> **AND **a conclusion that a precipitate forms

> **[exam-tip]**
> When two equal volumes are mixed, each concentration is halved. Use: c<sub>mixed</sub> = c<sub>original</sub> x V<sub>original</sub> / V<sub>total</sub>.
> 
> If IP > *K*<sub>sp</sub>, the solution is supersaturated and a precipitate forms. If IP < *K*<sub>sp</sub>, no precipitate forms.
